question: [RETRY of 429-refused question] Why does the Transformer scale dot-product attention by $1/\sqrt{d_k}$, and what are the exact dimensions $h$, $d_{\text{model}}$, $d_k$, $d_v$, and $d_{ff}$ in the base model?
expected: For large $d_k$, dot products grow large in magnitude (if components of $q$ and $k$ are independent random variables with mean $0$ and variance $1$, their dot product has mean $0$ and variance $d_k$), pushing the softmax function into regions with extremely small gradients; scaling by $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ counteracts this (Attention Is All You Need, Sec. 3.2.1, Footnote 1). The base model uses $h=8$ heads, $d_{\text{model}}=512$, $d_k=d_v=d_{\text{model}}/h=64$, and inner feed-forward dimension $d_{ff}=2048$ across $N=6$ encoder and decoder layers (Sec. 3.1, 3.2.2, 3.3, Table 3).
reply: The Transformer scales dot‑product attention by \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) to prevent the raw dot products of the query and key vectors from growing too large as the dimensionality \(d_k\) increases.  When the components of the queries and keys are independent random variables with mean zero and variance one, their dot product has variance \(d_k\).  Without scaling, the softmax would be pushed into its extreme tails, yielding very small gradients and making training difficult.  Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) normalises the variance of the dot product to be approximately one, keeping the softmax in a region with reasonable gradients and stabilising training.  This scaling is explicitly mentioned in the description of the scaled dot‑product attention in §3.2.1. question: In Moshi's safety evaluation, why does AudioSeal signal-based watermarking fail when tested against Mimi, why does token-level generative watermarking also fail, and how does Moshi eliminate verbatim training-data regurgitation?

Generative token-sampling watermarks also fail because Mimi is not idempotent: re-encoding a generated waveform changes token indices (even at $\Delta T = 0$, only $76.6\%$ of semantic $k=1$ tokens and $26.4\%–55.0\%$ of acoustic $k=2..8$ tokens match, dropping to $48.3\%$ for $k=1$ under a $40\text{ ms}$ shift) (Sec. 6.4, Table 16). To prevent regurgitation of frequent training segments (which reaches $98.4\%–100\%$ on 3s-prompted raw single-stream models), Moshi deduplicates the training audio using mel-spectrogram constellation-map hashes ($2^{26}$ hash space with Hough 1D temporal voting, Appendix B), reducing the regurgitation rate to $0.00\%$ across $10^5$ generations (Sec. 6.2, Table 13, Appendix B).
reply: Token‑level generative watermarking also fails in the Moshi pipeline because the codec that maps audio to discrete tokens is not idempotent. When a waveform is generated from tokens and then re‑encoded back into tokens, the resulting token sequence changes due to the codec’s quantization process, especially for higher‑level residual quantizers. This instability means that the hash‑based sampling bias used by generative watermarking cannot be reliably detected after re‑encoding. Table 16 shows that the probability of a token remaining identical after decoding and re‑encoding decreases sharply with higher residual‑quantizer levels and is further reduced by modest temporal shifts or by RVQGAN re‑encoding. Hence the necessary stability for the watermark detection mechanism is lacking. [moshi-B-050][moshi-B-051][Part of this answer was withheld because it could not be checked against the papers.]
